title: Discovering the Woman Within

modules.title: Knowing Who You Are
modules.overview: Discovering the Woman Within: Knowing Who You Are. Study each session, complete the reflection and practical output, and pass the module quiz before moving forward.

blocks.text: Introduction Think about the compound or the house you grew up in. You have walked through it thousands of times. But have you ever walked through it slowly, on purpose, looking closely at every room, noticing what is really there? Most of us have never done that with our own compound. And most of us have never done it with ourselves either. That is what this study session is asking you to do. Not to judge yourself. Not to praise yourself either. Just to look, honestly, at the woman you already are, the good parts and the parts still under construction, so that everything WODDI helps you build after this rests on something true. A title, a certificate, a big role in your church or mosque or community, none of that can stand in for actually knowing who you are underneath it.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 14. Explain, in your own words, what it means to look at yourself honestly. 15. Name the four things that make up self-knowledge: your experiences, your patterns, your strengths and limits, and your needs and hopes. 16. Try one practice of self-observation on a real situation from your own life this week. 17. Tell the difference between honest self-knowledge and simply feeling bad about yourself.
Main Content
What Do We Mean by "Knowing Yourself"?

Self-knowledge is simply the ability to look at your own life and describe it truthfully. Your experiences. Your habits. What you are genuinely good at, and where you still need to grow. What you need, and what you hope for. All of it, described honestly, without making yourself smaller than you are and without making yourself bigger than you are either. This is not a personality quiz you take once and forget. It is a habit of paying attention. And here is something worth hearing clearly: you do not need a crisis or a dramatic turning point to begin. Amara, a first-year student in Enugu, started simply by asking herself one question every Sunday evening: what actually happened this week, and what did it teach me? That is all self-knowledge takes to begin.
Why We Start Here, Before Anything Else

A lot of young women learn how to look confident before they ever learn who they really are underneath the confidence. They know how to speak well in a meeting, how to dress for the room, how to say the right thing at the right time. But underneath all of that, many have never actually sat down and asked themselves what is true about their own life.

That gap does not stay hidden forever. It shows up eventually, usually at the exact moment a woman is finally given real responsibility, and discovers she has been performing a version of herself she does not fully know. WODDI wants to help you close that gap now, quietly, while the stakes are still small, rather than later, when they are not. A psychologist named Carl Rogers spent his career studying this exact gap. He noticed that people feel most at peace when there is very little distance between who they actually are and who they feel they are supposed to be (Rogers, 1961). Another pair of researchers, Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham, built something called the Johari Window (1955), a simple idea really: some things about you, you and everyone around you both see clearly. Some things others notice about you that you have never noticed yourself. This is exactly why one of this session's practices asks you to invite honest feedback. It is often the fastest way to see what has been sitting in plain sight the whole time.
The Four Things Self-Knowledge Is Made Of

Self-knowledge is not one big mysterious thing. It is made of four smaller, very ordinary things. Your Experiences, and What They Actually Taught You Every experience, the ones that went well and the ones that did not, is carrying a lesson somewhere inside it. Take Blessing, a single mother who runs a small hairdressing stall in a semi-urban town outside Ibadan. She applied to lead her trade association's youth committee and did not get chosen. She could have simply concluded she was not good enough. She could have simply concluded the whole process was unfair. Instead, she asked herself a more useful question: setting aside how the decision was made, what does this actually show me about my preparation, or how I presented myself, or my timing? That question, not the disappointment itself, is what she carried forward. Your Patterns One event tells you very little on its own. But a habit, a feeling or a choice that keeps repeating itself is trying to tell you something important. If you have felt overlooked at home, then at school, then again in your youth group, that feeling showing up three separate times is now more worth examining than any one of those moments alone. Your Strengths and Your Limits, Held Together Many of us fall into one of two habits. Either we only ever talk about our strengths, afraid that admitting a weakness will make us look bad. Or we only ever talk about our limits, unable to say one good thing about ourselves without feeling embarrassed. Neither one is honest self-knowledge. Both are a kind of hiding. Real self-observation holds both truths in the same hand at once. You have real strength, and you still have real growing to do, and neither one cancels the other out. This is not some foreign idea borrowed from a psychology textbook. It is the same wisdom many of our own mothers and grandmothers have always carried, raising daughters to be proud and teachable in the same breath. It also helps to be specific. "I work hard" does not say very much. "I keep showing up to finish what I started, even after the excitement of starting it has worn off" says a great deal. The second sentence points to something a person can actually see and trust. Your Needs and Your Hopes

Finally, self-knowledge includes being honest about what you actually need, and what you actually hope for. This is not selfish. It is simply information, the kind you need in order to make good decisions about your relationships, your studies, your work and how you serve other people.
Ways to Practise This, Starting This Week

Here are three things you can actually do, whether you live in a village, a small town or a big city. •   Once a week, look back at something significant that happened, and ask yourself honestly what it taught you. •   Pay attention to what keeps repeating in your life, a feeling, a habit, a choice, and take it seriously. •   Ask one trustworthy person, someone who genuinely wants good for you, what they see in you that you may be missing. None of this needs to feel dramatic. A woman who does this quietly, in the middle of an ordinary week, is doing exactly the work this session is asking for.
Being Honest Without Being Harsh

Self-knowledge should leave you with clarity and a next step, not a heavy feeling of shame that goes nowhere. If a past mistake taught you something, hold on to the lesson. Let go of treating that mistake as a permanent verdict on who you are. At the same time, self-knowledge is not permission to describe yourself as better than the evidence actually shows. The goal is simply accuracy, held with dignity. Here is a simple way to check yourself. Honest reflection always leaves you with something specific to do differently. If you finish reflecting and all you feel is heaviness, with nothing clear to act on, pause. You may have slipped from self-knowledge into self-punishment, and it is worth returning to these practices to find your way back. A researcher named Kristin Neff (2011) makes a useful distinction here, between self-compassion, treating yourself the way you would treat a friend you love, and self-esteem, which can rise and fall with comparison and achievement. Self-knowledge held with compassion can absorb an honest limitation without collapsing into shame.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

You learned that self-knowledge is made of four ordinary things: your experiences, your patterns, your strengths and limits, and your needs and hopes, and that the goal is honesty held with dignity, not shame. You practised reviewing a real experience, noticing a repeating pattern, and asking someone you trust what they see in you. Study Session 2 builds directly on this, moving from knowing yourself to understanding your particular style.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 18. What is one thing about yourself that you have known for a while but never said out loud? 19. Think of a habit, feeling or choice that has shown up more than once in your life. What might it be telling you? 20. Who is one person you trust enough to ask what they honestly see in you? Practical Output: Practical Output Write a one-page personal identity map: your strengths, the areas you are still growing in, one or two experiences that shaped you, and what matters most to you right now.
References and Further Reading

•   Rogers, C. R. (1961). On Becoming a Person. Boston: Houghton Mifflin. •   Luft, J. and Ingham, H. (1955). The Johari Window, a simple framework for understanding self-awareness and feedback. •   Neff, K. (2011). Self-Compassion. New York: William Morrow. •   Psalm 139:14, an optional reading for those who find encouragement in scripture. •   Qur'an 91:7-8 (Surah Ash-Shams), an optional reading for those who find encouragement in scripture, on the soul and its awareness of right and wrong.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction Every family has that one relative who talks to everyone at a party, and another who quietly finds one person to sit with and have a real conversation. Neither one is doing it wrong. They are simply wired differently, and both of them can be excellent company. This study session is about learning your own wiring. Not so you can put yourself in a box and stop growing, but so you can stop fighting who you naturally are, and start using it well. Whether you grew up in a quiet farming village or a noisy city, your personality travelled with you, and it is worth actually getting to know.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 21. Describe your own personality as a set of natural tendencies, not a fixed label. 22. Notice how you typically get your energy, communicate and make decisions. 23. Tell the difference between how you act normally and how you act when you are under pressure. 24. Practise adjusting how you communicate to fit a situation, without pretending to be a different person.
Main Content
Building on What You Already Started

In Study Session 1, you started paying honest attention to your experiences and patterns. This session takes that same attention and points it somewhere specific, your personality, the natural tendencies that shape how you get your energy, how you talk to people, how you make decisions, and how you respond when things get difficult.
A Set of Tendencies, Not a Cage

Your personality is a set of tendencies, a natural rhythm that keeps showing up in how you operate. It grows and adjusts as you do; nobody else gets to lock you inside it. Some women come alive in a room full of people and conversation. Others come alive in quiet, with space to think. Neither one is better. They are just different starting points. There is a temptation worth naming here. A quiet, thoughtful woman watches a loud, expressive leader on stage and decides she must become louder to be respected. A direct, fast-moving woman watches someone calm and measured and decides she must slow herself down completely to be taken seriously. WNNN is not asking you to trade in your own wiring for someone else's. Learn your own well enough to lead from it with skill, and keep growing in the places every style needs to stretch.

People have studied personality for a long time. In the 1920s, Carl Jung noticed that people have fairly consistent preferences in how they take in the world and make decisions, ideas that later shaped tools like the Myers-Briggs. More recent researchers, Costa and McCrae (1992), describe personality along five broad dimensions rather than fixed types, which fits well with what this study session is teaching you: personality is a spectrum, not a box.
Four Things Worth Noticing About Yourself

Where do you get your energy? Some women feel most alive in a busy market surrounded by people; others feel most alive with a quiet hour and a notebook. Neither drains a woman who understands it. What only drains her is not knowing which one she is. How do you naturally communicate? Some of us speak our minds the moment a thought arrives. Others need to sit with an idea first before we are ready to share it. Both can be equally clear and equally kind, they simply arrive at different speeds. How do you usually decide? Some of us lead with logic and facts first. Others lead with how a decision will affect the people involved. A wise decision usually needs both eventually, but most of us have a natural starting point. And finally, how do you behave under pressure, compared to how you behave normally? Ngozi, who works at a small clinic on the edge of Kumasi, is usually warm and easy to talk to. But under a sudden deadline, she has noticed she becomes sharp and closed off, almost unrecognisable to herself. That is not a new personality showing up. That is her stress state, and simply being able to name it helps her catch herself and recover faster. Researchers call this the difference between a trait, your stable tendency, and a state, how you behave in a particular moment (Fleeson, 2001).
What You Can Actually Do With This

Try these over the next few weeks. •   Notice, honestly, which of your natural preferences show up again and again. •   Watch what happens to your style when you are under real pressure, and name it when it happens. •   Practise adjusting how you communicate to fit the room, without erasing who you actually are underneath it. •   Ask someone close to you what they notice about how you change under stress, since they often see it before you do.
A Tool for Understanding Yourself, Not an Excuse

Personality tools are meant to help you understand yourself, not give you permission to behave badly. If a woman says "I am just direct" to justify being unkind, or "I am just quiet" to avoid doing something brave that is required of her, she has turned a useful tool into a hiding place. No personality type is superior to another, and none of them excuses harmful behaviour. Every style, pushed too far, becomes a weakness. Directness, unchecked, becomes harshness. Warmth, unchecked, struggles to hold a boundary. Caution, unchecked, becomes paralysis. Boldness, unchecked,
becomes recklessness. Knowing your personality is not the finish line. It is the start of an honest, lifelong conversation with yourself about which edges of your own style deserve the most care.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

You learned to see your personality as a set of natural tendencies rather than a fixed box, covering how you gain energy, communicate, decide and respond under pressure. You practised noticing your preferences and telling the difference between your normal self and your stressed self. Study Session 3 goes one layer deeper still, into the emotional life running underneath your personality.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 25. Do you tend to get your energy from being around people, or from quiet time alone? What tells you this about yourself? 26. Describe a moment recently when pressure changed how you normally act. What did you notice? Practical Output: Practical Output Complete a personality reflection using an approved tool, and write down two strengths and two growth areas that came out of it.
References and Further Reading

•   Jung, C. G. (1921). Psychological Types. Zurich: Rascher Verlag. •   Costa, P. T. and McCrae, R. R. (1992). Revised NEO Personality Inventory. Odessa: Psychological Assessment Resources. •   Fleeson, W. (2001). Toward a Structure- and Process-Integrated View of Personality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80(6). •   16Personalities (NERIS Analytics), a free, widely used personality-preference reflection.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction Many of us were taught one of two things about our feelings growing up. Either that they are dangerous and should be hidden, especially in front of others. Or that whatever we feel in the moment must be the truth, and must be acted on immediately. This study session offers you a third way, one that is more useful than either. A feeling is information, something to read carefully rather than either swallow whole or hide away. A woman who can name what she feels, trace where it came from, and then decide how to respond has put her feelings to work for her. They stay hers to direct.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 27. Explain how a feeling connects to a bodily sensation, a thought, a need and finally an action. 28. Practise naming an emotion accurately, right when it happens. 29. Identify what triggered a strong feeling, and the story your mind attached to it. 30. Choose a response to a feeling that matches your values, rather than reacting automatically. 31. Explain why a strong feeling is not, on its own, proof that your interpretation is correct.
Main Content
One Layer Deeper

You have looked honestly at your patterns, and you have started to understand your personality. This study session takes you one layer deeper still, into your emotional life, the feelings running underneath both of the sessions before this one.
What Emotional Self-Awareness Actually Means

Being emotionally self-aware means noticing what you feel clearly enough to name it, rather than being carried along by it without understanding it. It has nothing to do with how much emotion a woman shows on the outside. A woman who says "I'm fine" while she is quietly falling apart inside is not practising self- awareness. She is practising avoidance, and there is a real difference. Some of us grew up in homes or communities where a strong feeling, especially in a woman or girl, was something to manage quickly and quietly, so as not to disturb anyone else. If that sounds familiar, this study session is not asking you to throw away your composure. It is asking you to stop confusing composure with honesty. You can remain calm, respectful and steady on the outside, while still being fully aware, on the inside, of what you actually feel. That composure becomes something you choose, not something you hide behind.

Two psychologists, Peter Salovey and John Mayer, gave this ability a name in 1990: emotional intelligence, the capacity to notice, understand and manage feeling, in yourself and in others. Daniel Goleman later made the idea widely known (1995), arguing that this kind of intelligence predicts real success in life at least as strongly as book intelligence does, sometimes more.
Following the Trail from Feeling to Action

Naming the feeling comes first, and it is harder than it sounds. Frustration, disappointment, embarrassment and anger can all feel almost identical in the body, but they call for very different responses. Getting the name right is the beginning of responding well. Every strong feeling has a trigger, the actual event that set it off, and a story, the meaning your mind attaches to that event. Think about Aisha, a young civil servant in a mid-sized town, who feels sidelined when a colleague is given a project she wanted. The trigger is the assignment decision. The story her mind tells her might be, "I am being overlooked because I am not valued." That story might be true. It might not be. Simply recognising it as a story, and not as settled fact, gives her room to check it before she acts on it. Feeling shows up in the body before the mind has fully caught up with it, a tight chest, a hot face, a knot low in the stomach. Learning to notice these early signals gives you a head start on naming the feeling before it grows big enough to take over. Once Aisha has named the feeling and questioned the story, she can ask what she actually needs, maybe clarity from her supervisor, maybe recognition for a different contribution, and act on that real need directly, instead of acting out of the raw feeling itself. A neuroscientist named Antonio Damasio (1994) found that the body often registers emotional information before conscious thought fully catches up, which is exactly why that tight chest or hot face tends to arrive before you have consciously worked out what you are feeling.
Building the Habit

Three small practices, done consistently, change how you handle your feelings over time. •   Pause, and put an accurate name on what you are feeling. •   Ask yourself what actually triggered it, and what story you are telling yourself about it. •   Choose a response that matches your values, rather than reacting on autopilot.
A Feeling Is Information, Not a Verdict

A strong feeling gives you real information, but it is not automatic proof that your interpretation is correct. Feeling betrayed does not, on its own, prove that betrayal actually happened. Take the feeling seriously enough to examine it, and hold the story behind it loosely enough to test it against the evidence. One good way to test a story is to describe it to someone you trust before you act on it, using the same kind of honest feedback you practised seeking in Study Session 1. If their honest read of the situation matches yours, your interpretation likely has real weight. If it does not, that gap is worth sitting with a little longer before you speak or act. It does not mean your feeling was wrong. It means the situation deserves a second, closer look.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

You learned to name feelings accurately, trace them back to their trigger and story, notice the bodily signals underneath them, and connect feeling to a real need and a chosen action. You practised pausing before reacting and testing your interpretations with someone you trust. Study Session 4 takes this same honesty and applies it to one specific, very common trigger: comparison.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 32. Which feeling is hardest for you to name honestly, even to yourself? 33. Think of a recent moment when you felt strongly about something. What was the trigger, and what story did your mind attach to it? 34. Describe a time you paused before reacting. What changed because of that pause? Practical Output: Practical Output Keep a three-day log of your feelings: what happened, what you felt, what triggered it, how you responded, and what a healthier response could have looked like.
References and Further Reading

•   Salovey, P. and Mayer, J. D. (1990). Emotional Intelligence. Imagination, Cognition and Personality, 9(3). •   Goleman, D. (1995). Emotional Intelligence. New York: Bantam Books. •   Damasio, A. (1994). Descartes' Error. New York: Putnam. •   Proverbs 4:23, an optional reading for those who find encouragement in scripture. •   Hadith of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, on the soundness of the heart, an optional reading for those who find encouragement in scripture.

blocks.text: Introduction If you have kept the emotion log from the last study session, there is a good chance one trigger showed up more than once: comparison. It shows up in classrooms, in workplaces, in church and mosque groups, on social media, and sometimes even inside our own families. This study session names comparison directly, and gives you something sturdier to stand on instead. WODDI wants you to be able to walk into any room, however senior, however unfamiliar, carrying a confidence that comes from your own dignity and your own preparation, one that never needs another woman to shrink so you can feel tall.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 35. Explain confidence as something rooted in dignity and preparation, rather than in being better than someone else. 36. Recognise comparison as a common trigger that can push a person toward either pride or insecurity. 37. Use your own progress, not someone else's, as your measuring stick. 38. Practise genuinely celebrating another woman's success.
Main Content
From Feeling to Standing Firm

The last study session gave you tools for naming feelings and tracing where they came from. One of the most common feelings a woman will meet, in school, at work, in her community, is comparison. This study session builds a specific, practical answer to it: confidence rooted in dignity and preparation, not in outranking anyone.
Where Real Confidence Actually Comes From

Confidence, the way this course teaches it, does not depend on where you land compared to another woman. It depends on your dignity, which nobody can hand you and nobody can take away, and on your preparation, which you can always keep building no matter what anyone else around you is doing. Social media has made comparison feel almost constant for young women today, a highlight reel of other women's achievements, bodies, relationships and opportunities, with all the struggle behind them carefully cut out. WNNN is not asking you to withdraw from your community to protect your confidence. It is asking you to remember, every time comparison rises up in you, that what you are seeing is a highlight, not the whole story, and that your own preparation is happening on a timeline nobody else can fully see either.

A social psychologist named Leon Festinger studied this back in 1954, and found that people naturally measure themselves against others, especially when there is no clear, objective way to know how they are doing. That is useful to know, because it means comparison is not a personal weakness unique to you. It is simply something almost everyone's mind does automatically. Brené Brown's research on shame (2012) adds something else worth knowing, that comparison grows strongest in secrecy, and tends to lose its grip once it is spoken out loud inside a trustworthy community, which is exactly why Learning Circles matter so much in this course.
Two Things to Hold Onto

Dignity is not a prize you win for being the best person in the room. It is the ground you already stand on before you have proven anything at all, and it does not get smaller just because another woman is further along, more visible or more accomplished than you are right now. Preparation is what keeps confidence from collapsing the first time it is actually tested. Doing the quiet work first means that when the real opportunity comes, your confidence has something solid underneath it, instead of nothing but hope.
A Story Worth Sitting With

In one Learning Circle spanning Abuja and Nairobi, two women found themselves stuck in very different traps. One kept outperforming the others and slowly began to feel superior, quietly looking down on the rest of the group. The other kept measuring herself against the strongest woman in the room and slowly began to feel she would never measure up. Neither one was actually using her own standard. Both were using someone else's, and both paid for it, one with quiet pride, the other with quiet insecurity. Comparison, this study session teaches, tends to pull in one of these two directions, and both pull equally hard against real growth.
Practising This for Yourself

Try noticing which direction you personally lean under comparison, since most of us have a default setting. •   Measure your progress against where you stood last month, not against another woman's current position. •   Practise celebrating another woman's growth out loud, especially if pride is your default lean. •   If insecurity is your default lean, practise naming your own progress out loud until it stops feeling strange.
Guarding Both Sides at Once

Real sisterhood, the kind WNNN is built on, means guarding against both directions comparison can pull you, the pride that looks down, and the insecurity that shrinks you. Both are worth watching for, not just the one that feels more familiar to you.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

You learned to root your confidence in dignity and preparation instead of comparison, and to notice comparison's two common traps: pride and insecurity. You practised measuring your own progress, celebrating other women, and preparing quietly before seeking visibility. Study Session 5 takes this same
confidence and asks what it looks like to build a steady sense of your own worth, one that holds even when no one is watching.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 39. Where have you let someone else's pace or timing quietly define your own sense of worth? 40. What personal standard, rather than someone else's, could you use to measure your own progress this month? 41. Describe a recent moment when comparison pulled you toward pride or toward insecurity. 42. Who is one woman whose success you could celebrate out loud this week? Practical Output: Practical Output Write down three situations where comparison tends to trigger you, and one practical, different response you could try for each.
References and Further Reading

•   Festinger, L. (1954). A Theory of Social Comparison Processes. Human Relations, 7(2). •   Brown, B. (2012). Daring Greatly. New York: Gotham Books. •   Brown, B. (2010). The Power of Vulnerability. TED Talk.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction The last study session helped you build confidence for specific moments, a task you have prepared for, a room you are walking into. This one goes broader and quieter: a settled sense of your own worth that stays with you even on days when nobody is testing you, watching you or applauding you. Many of us grew up hearing one of two messages about our own worth. Either that any sense of self-worth is dangerous pride, to be guarded against at every turn. Or that worth has to be earned all over again each day through performance. WODDI wants to offer you something steadier than either one: worth that stays put because it is built on truth, not on applause.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 43. Explain healthy self-esteem as holding both your dignity and your need to keep growing, at the same time. 44. Practise speaking to yourself honestly, without either harshness or empty flattery. 45. Set small commitments to yourself and actually keep them. 46. Receive both praise and correction without losing your footing. 47. Tell healthy self-esteem apart from entitlement, perfectionism and pretending you have no weaknesses at all.
Main Content
From a Moment to a Foundation

Confidence, built in Study Session 4, often responds to a specific moment. Self-esteem is quieter and wider than that. It is the steady sense of your own worth that stays present even on the days nobody is watching, testing or applauding you at all.
Holding Two Truths at Once

Healthy self-esteem holds your dignity and your need to keep growing together, without letting either one push the other out. You are already worth something. You are also still becoming who you will be. Both are true at the same time; one does not shrink the other. This matters because many of us are only ever handed one half of this truth. Some environments teach a woman she has to earn her worth all over again every single day, through achievement or appearance or endless service, leaving her sense of self as fragile as her last success. Other environments hand out only empty praise, insisting she is already perfect, which leaves her unable to receive the honest correction that real growth actually requires.

A researcher named Morris Rosenberg built one of the most widely used tools for measuring self-worth back in 1965, and decades of research building on his work has found something worth knowing, that healthy self-esteem works best as something steady, not something that swings up and down with your mood each day. Another researcher, Nathaniel Branden (1994), studied what actually builds lasting self- esteem, and found practices strikingly close to what this study session teaches, honest self-acceptance, taking responsibility for yourself, and living with integrity.
Three Habits Worth Building

Speak to yourself honestly, in language that is accurate and kind at the same time, rather than harsh criticism on one side or empty flattery on the other. Set small commitments to yourself, and keep them. This is how self-trust is actually built, evidence gathered over time, not affirmation alone. When Chidinma, a young teacher in a rural school outside Kigali, received glowing feedback on her lesson one week and a difficult performance note the next, she found she could hold both as true and useful, without either one deciding her entire sense of worth. That is what receiving praise and correction well actually looks like.
What Healthy Self-Esteem Is Not Confused With

It is worth being clear about three things healthy self-esteem often gets mistaken for. Entitlement is believing you deserve good outcomes without putting in the effort. Perfectionism is believing you must never be seen to fail at anything. And pretending you have no weaknesses at all is simply refusing to admit any limitation, ever. Each of these can look like confidence from a distance, but none of them can hold up under real pressure the way genuine self-esteem can.
Standing on Two Feet

Refusing to choose between your dignity and your growth is the heart of healthy self-esteem. A woman who only claims her dignity, without ever accepting she still has growing to do, drifts toward entitlement over time. A woman who only chases growth, without ever resting in the dignity she already has, drifts toward exhaustion and quietly rejecting herself. WODDI is asking you to hold both, always, together. Picture a woman standing on two feet instead of balancing on one. Standing only on dignity, with no weight on growth, she becomes still and satisfied with herself in a way that stops her moving forward. Standing only on growth, with no weight on dignity, she becomes restless, never quite settled. Standing on both at once is far less dramatic than either extreme, but it is what lets a woman walk steadily for a lifetime, rather than stumbling from one imbalance into the other.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

You learned that healthy self-esteem holds dignity and growth together, and you practised honest self- talk, keeping small commitments, and receiving both praise and correction with steadiness. You also learned to tell it apart from entitlement, perfectionism and pretending you have no weaknesses. Study Session 6 brings everything from this course together into one authentic, values-aligned life.

Introduction You have now walked through five study sessions: looking honestly at yourself, understanding your personality, naming your feelings, building confidence that does not depend on comparison, and settling into a steady sense of your own worth. This last study session is not adding something new. It is asking you to bring all of it together, into one life where what you believe, what you say, what you choose and how you treat people actually match. This is what WODDI means by becoming more, becoming ready: a woman who is recognisably the same person in every room she walks into, still learning, still growing, no longer pulled in two directions at once.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 51. Explain authenticity as your values, words, choices and relationships all pointing the same direction, consistently. 52. Practise stating a conviction respectfully, in a real conversation. 53. Make one choice that visibly reflects a value you have named. 54. Tell authenticity apart from saying every single thing you feel, and from refusing all correction. 55. Bring together what you built in Study Sessions 1 through 5 into one honest statement about who you are becoming. 56. Describe what it will look like to keep practising this authenticity in the courses that follow.
Main Content
Where the Five Study Sessions Meet

Each study session in this course has added one layer, honest self-observation, understanding your personality, emotional self-awareness, confidence without comparison, and healthy self-esteem. This one is where they all meet. You cannot align a life you have not first examined, which is exactly why this study session comes last, not first.
What Authenticity Actually Means

Authenticity is alignment: your values, the words you use, the choices you make and the way you show up with people, all pointing in the same direction, consistently, across different rooms and different seasons of your life. Saying whatever crosses your mind is something else entirely, and section 2.4 comes back to that distinction. Notice that word, consistently. A woman can be warm with her family and cold with strangers, generous when people are watching and resentful in private, confident with her mentors and dismissive toward people she supervises. Every one of these is a kind of inconsistency, and each one is quietly telling on

something underneath that has not yet lined up. Becoming authentically you is the ordinary, daily work of closing these gaps, one relationship and one room at a time, until you are recognisably the same woman wherever you go. Two researchers, Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, found in 1985 that acting from your own genuine values, rather than from outside pressure, is one of a small number of basic psychological needs every person has. Later, Michael Kernis and Brian Goldman (2006) mapped authenticity into four parts, knowing yourself, seeing your own strengths and weaknesses clearly, behaving consistently, and being honest in your relationships. Look closely and you will notice those four parts track almost exactly onto the five study sessions you have just finished.
What This Looks Like in Practice

Speak your convictions clearly, without needing to raise your voice, and without softening them into silence just to be liked. Values that only ever get spoken out loud, and never actually chosen, are not authenticity yet. They are hopes. A woman who says she values honesty but bends the truth whenever it is convenient has a real gap between what she says and what she does. Closing that gap, one choice at a time, is the daily practice authenticity actually asks of you. Funke, who had genuinely grown in confidence since Study Session 4, noticed she was starting to feel pressure to perform that confidence constantly, even on the days she did not actually feel it, just so people would notice her progress. Real growth does not need an audience. It keeps happening quietly, on the days nobody is watching, because it belongs to her, not to how she looks to others.
What Authenticity Is Not

Authenticity does not mean saying everything you feel, to everyone, in every setting. And it does not mean refusing wise correction because it feels like an attack on who you are. A woman who says something hurtful and defends it as "just being real" has confused authenticity with a lack of self-control.
A Practice, Not a Finish Line

Authenticity is not a trophy you win once and keep forever. It is an ongoing practice, one that will be tested again in every course still ahead of you in Blueprint Academy. The woman you are becoming through this course is not a finished product. She is a foundation. There is a saying that comes from Ubuntu, an idea widely shared by Archbishop Desmond Tutu (1999): a person only becomes fully themselves through their relationships with others. Authenticity, in that tradition, is never a purely private matter. It shows up in how honestly and respectfully you treat the people around you, which is exactly why this study session ties authenticity to your relationships as much as to what is going on inside you.
Where You Go From Here

You began this course learning to look at yourself honestly. You are ending it by bringing that honesty, together with your personality, your emotional awareness, your confidence and your self-esteem, into one authentic life. That is the woman WODDI has been helping you become through these six study

sessions, not a performance, not a label, but a woman who knows who she is, what she stands for, and the purpose she is preparing to carry. Carry her forward into Course 2, Designed for Purpose, and into every course after it. Nothing ahead of you will ask you to leave her behind. She is the one who keeps walking through all of it, becoming more, becoming ready.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

You learned that authenticity means your values, words, choices and relationships all pointing the same direction, built on everything from the five study sessions before this one. You practised speaking convictions respectfully, making value-aligned choices, and letting growth happen without needing an audience. This closes Course 1 and prepares you for the Identity and Purpose Portfolio, and for Course 2.
